text: Effect boundaries. A doeff program runs in two zones: inside doeff, and outside it.
Inside, the handler stack answers each effect, with k, the rest of the program. Outside, Python's event loop runs your coroutines.
Almost every effect stays inside. Await is the one that crosses the line.
Here is the page's pipeline: Ask, Spawn, Gather, Wait and Try, and each worker's Get, Put and Tell.
An observer handler sees all fifteen effects go by. Each one is answered by a handler inside doeff.
All of it runs on one thread, with no event loop at all. Even the tasks are just the scheduler handler's work.
Await is different. Python's await is syntax, and it only runs under an event loop.
await handler hands each coroutine to an event loop on its own thread, the await bridge, and the scheduler parks the task's k.
While A and B are outside, task C's steps are still answered inside doeff, all before either coroutine returns.
B's coroutine returns at about a hundred milliseconds, and its k resumes. A follows at two hundred: about two hundred in all, not three.
Waiting inside doeff is scheduler suspension: a handler holds the task's k, and resumes it later.
A Wait on a promise another task completes takes under two milliseconds. A three second Delay on the virtual clock, under one.
An Await of a point three second sleep takes three hundred milliseconds of real time, answered on the bridge thread. Only that wait leaves doeff.
Your own handlers keep the boundary strict. Here is one program, Fetch a URL, under two handlers.
from table answers inside doeff. over async needs Python async, so it performs Await itself.
That Await travels outward, so await handler goes outside over async, and scheduled outside both.
Leave await handler out, or put it on the inside, and the Await finds no handler.
So answer domain effects in handlers, cross only for real async work, and leave task switching to the scheduler.
doeff: effects are answered by handlers, inside doeff. Await is the one door out, to Python's event loop. pip install doeff.
